content.title: Immunizations: Measles
content.text: Measles is a disease caused by the measles virus. Measles can be dangerous, especially for infants and young children.One out of every four people who get measles in the United States will be hospitalized. One or two out of every 1,000 children in the United States who get measles will die from the disease, even with the best care.Measles can cause serious health problems, such as:Pneumonia, an infection of the lungs.Brain damage caused by swelling.Deafness.You can protect yourself and the people around you from measles. The best protection against measles is a measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR or MMRV) vaccine.Two doses of the measles vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles. The vaccine provides long-lasting protection against all strains of measles.Measles 101Measles cases in WisconsinMeasles cases in Wisconsinites by week, age, and county. This data will be updated weekly on Tuesday.About our data: How do we measure this?This dashboard provides a breakdown of measles cases among Wisconsin residents by week, age, and county.Data source: The Wisconsin Electronic Disease Surveillance System (WEDSS).Measles cases: Include confirmed and probable cases by rash onset date.Confirmed case: A case with laboratory confirmation (measles-specific IgM antibodies, PCR, or viral isolation) or cases meeting the clinical case definition and linked epidemiologically to a confirmed case.Probable case: A case that meet the clinical case definition without laboratory confirmation or an epidemiologic link to a confirmed case.Case count: One case is one person.Note: All data in the dashboard are provisional and subject to change. The data in this dashboard will be updated on a weekly basis.Just for health care providersMeasles is a communicable disease.
